t: 3255. Find the Power of K-Size Subarrays II
o: A window is 'powered' iff its elements are strictly consecutive ascending (each element = previous + 1); then its power is its last (maximum) element, else -1. Sliding a window of size k across the array, we only need to know whether the run of consecutive increments ending at the window's right end covers the whole window. Example 1: runs 1,2,3 and 2,3,4 power windows 0 and 1; the rest fail consecutiveness or sortedness.
k: Track the length of the maximal consecutive-ascending run ending at each index.
Window [i, i+k-1] is powered iff that run length ≥ k.
Power equals nums[right] — the run's last element is the window max.

a.i: One pass maintaining `run`: reset to 1 on a broken increment, else increment. Whenever i ≥ k−1 and run ≥ k, record nums[i] at results[i−k+1]. Everything else stays −1 from initialization.
s: For i from 0: run = run+1 if nums[i] == nums[i-1]+1 else 1.
If i ≥ k-1 and run ≥ k, set results[i-k+1] = nums[i].
a.t: O(n) — single pass with constant updates

a.n: Approach 2: Prefix Sum of Good Adjacents
a.i: Define good[i] = 1 if nums[i] = nums[i-1]+1. Window [l, l+k-1] is powered iff the sum of good over (l+1 .. l+k-1) equals k-1. Prefix sums answer each window in O(1) after an O(n) build — conceptually cleaner for some, identical complexity.
s: Build prefix sums P of good[].
For each window start l: valid iff P[l+k-1] - P[l] == k-1.
If valid set results[l] = nums[l+k-1], else -1.
a.t: O(n) — prefix build plus one O(1) check per window

w: Both are linear; prefer the run-length scan for O(1) auxiliary space. Pitfall: treating equal adjacent elements (example 2's all-2s) as consecutive — they are not; also k = 1 makes every window powered. Follow-up: windows that are consecutive but descending, or k-th largest queries on arbitrary windows.
